title: Aisha's du'a
hook: O Allah, You are pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the odd nights, and your line: seek it. Did an argument come up, and did you let it go any sooner? Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

"What should I say?" That's Aisha's question, and it's a practical one. Yesterday's night, the Night of Power, is hidden somewhere in the last ten of Ramadan. Suppose she happens to know which night it is. Suppose she's standing in it. Out of everything a person could ask for on a night better than a thousand months, what should she say? She puts the question to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the answer is short enough to learn in a minute. Today, Aisha's du'a.
screen: `WHAT SHOULD I SAY?` → `IF I KNEW WHICH NIGHT.` → `A SHORT ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the source. The exchange is in the collection of al-Tirmidhi. Aisha asks; the Prophet tells her to say a single line. In Arabic: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun, tuhibbul 'afwa, fa'fu 'anni. In plain English, it calls Allah the one who pardons, says He loves to pardon, and asks Him to pardon her. That's all. Second, what it leaves out. No list of wishes. No health, no wealth, no request about the future. On the night the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months, the answer is one request, and it's for pardon. Third, the word itself. 'Afw, pardon. Some teachers explain it as more than forgiving: wiping a thing away so that no trace of it is left, the way wind wipes a track off sand. The hadith itself doesn't spell that out. What the hadith does spell out is the shape of the line. It doesn't begin with the person's need. It begins with who Allah is, the one who pardons. Then it says what He loves, to pardon. And only then does it ask. Name, then love, then the request. Fourth, how people use it. In the last ten nights, some Muslims repeat this line again and again, on every odd night, in case this is the one. It is said in Arabic, often quietly, between longer prayers. And it travels well outside Ramadan: a person can say it after a hard day, or after a mistake that's still stinging. One more thing, which belongs to Aisha. She didn't ask what the night would bring her. She asked what she should say. The question itself is part of the lesson.
screen: `ONE LINE, FROM AL-TIRMIDHI.` · `NO LIST OF WISHES.` · `NAME, THEN LOVE, THEN ASK.` · `SAID AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `TUHIBBUL 'AFWA.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it, or listen to it. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say Aisha's line now, slowly, in Arabic if you know it, or in your own language: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun, tuhibbul 'afwa, fa'fu 'anni. Say it once, and then sit with it. If you don't pray, notice its shape instead. Who is named first. What is loved. What is asked. And then think of one thing you'd be glad to have wiped away. Just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Aisha's du'a. The line the Prophet taught Aisha for the Night of Power, asking the one who loves to pardon for pardon. Today's word.

Your line: you love to pardon. Tonight, before you sleep, go back over the shape of the line once: who is named, what is loved, what is asked. Tomorrow: fasting safely. Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, some Muslims repeat Aisha's du'a many times, in Arabic, between other prayers, and some say it at other times of the year too.

fork.setup: you're Aisha. you think you may be standing in the Night of Power. what do you do?
options: ask the Prophet what you should say.
make a list of everything you want.
wait until morning to be sure.
fork.reveal: she asks what to say, and the answer is one line, asking the one who loves to pardon for pardon.

original.note: 'you love pardon', the heart of Aisha's du'a.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for forgiveness.
what it means: a line that names Allah as the one who pardons and loves to pardon, then asks for pardon.
what a scholar hears: 'afw, which some teachers explain as wiping a thing away so no trace is left.
recall: given in place of a fast

notes: Tirmidhi 3513: confirm number and grading. Some printed editions add 'karim' ('afuwwun karim); the shorter form is used here. Confirm the transliteration and the Arabic in the original game.
The English is a paraphrase, not a quotation, so no new wording of the prayer is presented as a translation.
The 'wiping away, like wind on sand' explanation of 'afw is offered as what some teachers say; a Keeper may prefer to name a source or cut the image.
